title: How data can build in bias

sections.skill: Explain how data can build in bias

questions.prompt: Why can problems in training data become problems in a model?

choices.text: Models learn patterns from the data

questions.correct_answer: Models learn patterns from the data
questions.intro: Models learn patterns from their TRAINING DATA, so problems in the data can become problems in the model. UNREPRESENTATIVE data leaves some groups out or underrepresents them: a skin-condition tool trained mostly on photos of light skin may work worse on dark skin. HISTORICAL data can carry past unfairness: if a company mostly promoted one group in the past, a model trained on its promotion records may learn to favor that group. The model is not "deciding" to be unfair; it repeats patterns. That is why data choices need careful checking.

sections.skill: Compare biased data with learning a language from one town

questions.prompt: What would you pick up from one town?

choices.text: Every accent and every way of speaking English in the whole world, equally well

questions.correct_answer: Its accent and local habits
questions.intro: Imagine learning English only from people in one small town. You would pick up their accent, local slang and habits, and you might struggle to understand people from elsewhere. That is not because other English is wrong; you just never heard it. A model trained on limited or skewed data is similar: it learns what it saw, and does worse on what it rarely saw.

questions.prompt: Why might you struggle with people from elsewhere?

questions.prompt: Labelers assume all nurses are women and label photos that way. Where did bias enter?

choices.text: In the computer hardware, which adds its own assumptions to every photo label

questions.correct_answer: In the labels
questions.intro: Bias can enter at every step, not only in data collection. LABELS can reflect labelers' assumptions. The question a model is asked to predict can be a poor stand-in for what matters: predicting "past arrests" is not the same as predicting "crimes committed," because arrests also reflect where police patrol. Fixing bias is rarely as simple as deleting one column; it usually takes better data, careful goals, testing across groups and ongoing monitoring.
